title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Ops Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
summary: Comprehensive reference for the Redwood serving runtime: architecture overview, kernel selection and scheduling heuristics, profiling playbook, benchmarking suite, known issues, runbooks for common incidents, and team wiki pointers.
content:
Overview

Purpose
This document is the single canonical reference for the Redwood serving runtime. It covers the runtime architecture, kernel scheduling and selection heuristics, profiling and performance-playbook, the canonical benchmarking suite and result format, notable known issues and mitigations, operational runbooks for common incidents, and links to the runtime team wiki and ownership.

Scope
- Production inference serving runtime used across Hosted, Dedicated and Private deployments.
- Includes GPU kernel selection, intra-node scheduler, batching and KV cache, and tracing/observability hooks.
- Intended audience: serving-runtime engineers, oncall SREs, performance owners, and release managers.

1) Architecture overview

High-level components
- Request ingress: API layer and edge routing (per-tenant routing policies). Responsible for authentication, tokenization and basic request validation.
- Orchestration layer: decides routing policy (latency/cost/region), model variant selection, and capacity/failover decisions.
- Serving runtime: the GPU-optimized inference engine that executes autoregressive models. Key subcomponents: kernel selector, kernel scheduler, continuous batching, KV cache, and execution backend.
- Observability: distributed tracing, token-level latency and cost breakdown, per-model dashboards and perf metrics ingestion.

Runtime responsibilities and invariants
- Maintain latency SLOs per route (default 99th percentile <= 200ms for small models; configured per-customer).
- Maximize throughput while keeping memory and GPU utilization under configured limits.
- Ensure graceful degradation: automatic fallback to cheaper model variants or lower-cost regions before dropping requests.

2) Kernel selection & scheduling

Goals
- Choose execution kernel (FP16/INT8/mixed-fp32 fused ops) that maximizes throughput within latency and memory constraints.
- Schedule kernels across CUDA streams and multiple GPUs (when model sharding) to reduce idle time and increase utilization.

Kernel selector (rules + profiles)
- Kernel candidates are scored using a cost function: score = alpha * latency_est + beta * memory_used + gamma * throughput_est + delta * quantization_penalty.
- Profiles are generated by the benchmarking suite and stored in the model catalog as per-architecture sequence-length buckets. Profiles include: latency per kernel, peak memory, recommended batch sizes, and warmup steps.
- Default configuration: prefer INT8 kernels for throughput-bound production workloads unless quality guardrails request FP16/FP32.

Scheduling heuristics
- Continuous batching: group concurrent requests using adaptive time-windowing with lower/upper batch size caps per model.
- Stream assignment: assign critical/low-latency tokens to high-priority CUDA streams; background bulk requests use lower-priority streams to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- Kernel preemption: short kernels (matrix-multiply heavy) are allowed to preempt long-latency kernels when doing canary traffic. Preemption follows a lease-style protocol to avoid deadlocks.
- Multi-GPU pipelining: for sharded models, use pipeline parallelism with elastic micro-batches and KV cache placement tied to tensor locality heuristics.

Config examples (engine config snippet)
- Model profile reference: model_profile: "gpt-3b-int8/seq-1024"
- Scheduling knobs (YAML-like):
  scheduler:
    max_batch_time_ms: 12
    min_batch_size: 1
    max_batch_size: 128
    low_latency_threshold_ms: 60
    stream_priority_map:
      critical: 3
      default: 2
      background: 1
    preemptible_kernels: ["gemm_small", "fused_attention_qkv"]

3) Profiling & performance playbook

When to profile
- After a release that touches runtime kernels, scheduler, or memory manager.
- When an SLO is breached for 3+ production samples or when perf regression alert fires.
- Before onboarding a new model into Dedicated or Private plans.

Tools and traces
- rwi-profiler (internal): lightweight sampling profiler that collects per-kernel timings, CUDA stream occupancy, SM utilization and memory peaks.
- nsys / Nsight Systems: end-to-end tracing for cross-process GPU timelines.
- nvprof (deprecated on newer stacks) / CUPTI events: fine-grained kernel counters.
- perf, eBPF traces for kernel scheduling and system-level metrics.

Profiling checklist (step-by-step)
1. Reproduce on a staging cluster that matches the production hardware profile.
2. Enable deterministic inputs: fixed prompt sets from the benchmarking suite (see section 4).
3. Run rwi-profiler with the same scheduling config and model profile. Collect 3 warm runs and 5 steady runs.
4. Capture Nsight timeline across the worker and driver processes for latency spikes.
5. Compare kernel breakdown (attention, ff, embedding, softmax) against baseline profile in the model catalog.
6. If memory pressure observed, enable memory logging and run a stress test to identify fragmentation or KV cache growth.
7. Create an artifact in the performance issue tracker with traces, rwi-profiler JSON, and a short hypothesis + mitigation.

Common profiling findings and mitigations
- Symptom: Many small kernels causing poor GPU utilization.
  Mitigation: fuse kernels where possible (build fused attention path) and increase micro-batch sizes for pipelining.
- Symptom: High kernel tail latency on attention.
  Mitigation: enable tiled attention kernels at long sequence lengths; verify kernel selection profile for that sequence bucket.
- Symptom: Spikes in CPU scheduling or blocking I/O.
  Mitigation: move non-critical work (metrics, logging) to background threads and increase buffer sizes for RPCs.

4) Benchmarking suite

Purpose
- Provide reproducible workloads, reference prompts, and result ingestion for model/kernel profiling and SLA verification.

Workloads and datasets
- Microbenchmarks: single-token latency (cold/warm), attention kernel microbenchmarks across sequence lengths [8,64,256,1024,2048].
- Macrobenchmarks: throughput across realistic mix: {0.6 chat-like short responses, 0.3 completion medium responses, 0.1 long-generation}.
- Regression prompts: curated eval prompt sets used by Redwood Optimize for quality/perf correlation.

Running the suite (CLI examples)
- ./bench/run_benchmark --model-profile gpt-3b-int8 --seq-lens 64,256,1024 --concurrency 32 --duration 600 --output results/gpt3b-2026-02-10.json

Result format (canonical schema)
- JSON fields: run_id, model_profile, hardware_profile, seq_len_bucket, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms, tokens_per_sec, max_memory_mb, kernel_breakdown (list of kernel->ms).
- Store results in the central perf bucket and link into the model catalog entry for that model_profile.

CI integration
- Benchmark suite runs on every PR that touches runtime kernels and before canary release. Baseline must show no > 5% regression in p95 latency or tokens/sec for production-critical models.

5) Release notes (runtime releases)

Format and expectations
- Each runtime release must include: summary of changes, affected components, performance/regression summary (benchmarks vs baseline), upgrade impact and rollback steps.
- Release checklist: run full benchmark suite on canary hardware, validate 3 canary tenants, run chaos tests for fallback and KV cache consistency.

Example (v2026.02.08)
- Summary: Add INT8 fused attention kernel and improve stream scheduling to reduce 99p tail by 18% for medium models.
- Affects: kernel selector, scheduling policy, model-profile database.
- Benchmarks: p95 reduced from 210ms -> 172ms on production canary for seq=256.
- Rollback: set SCHED_POLICY to legacy and restart worker; monitor p99 for 15 minutes.

6) Known issues and mitigations

- Issue: Intermittent KV cache corruption after aggressive evictions (observed on some 2-GPU shards).
  - Symptoms: incorrect outputs for long-context requests, increased log errors mentioning checksum failures.
  - Workaround: set cache_eviction_mode: safe-ttl (increases memory but avoids corruption) and restart worker. Patch is in review (PR #8342).
- Issue: CUDA driver OOM on model swap under high-concurrency spikes.
  - Symptoms: driver reset, worker crash loops, errors in dmesg.
  - Mitigation: enable reserve_gpu_pool: true and cap concurrent model-loads via admission controller.
- Issue: Kernel selection flips between INT8 and FP16 for the same workload causing output variance.
  - Mitigation: pin model_profile.runtime_kernel to a fixed kernel for the rollout window and add a quality check in canary gating.

7) Runbooks (high-level, step-by-step)

A) High 99p latency on production route
1. Check route-level dashboards for recent config changes and burst traffic.
2. Identify affected model_profile and query recent benchmark results.
3. Run rwi-profiler against a canary worker for 5 minutes.
4. If kernel tail times high, switch to lower-latency kernel in model_profile (hotfix) and perform canary traffic validation.
5. If memory pressure, enable emergency cache eviction policy and scale up worker pool.
6. Always notify oncall and create an incident timeline in the incident tracker.

B) Worker OOM / GPU driver reset
1. Move incoming traffic away from the affected instance by setting routing.tag: exclude-worker-<id>.
2. Collect /var/log/syslog, dmesg, and the worker trace (rwi-profiler).
3. If OOM triggered during model load, set admission_controller.load_limit = 1 and restart the worker.
4. If hardware issue, escalate to infra and mark host for hardware investigation.

C) KV cache corruption detected
1. Immediately enable safe-ttl cache mode for the affected shard(s).
2. Drain and restart the affected processes.
3. Run consistency checks against a golden trace for affected prompts.
4. Re-ingest traces to the bug ticket and notify the applied-ml team.

8) Observability and alerting (key metrics & SLOs)
- Key metrics: request_latency_p50/p95/p99, tokens_per_sec, gpu_utilization, sm_efficiency, kernel_tail_ms, kv_cache_hit_rate, memory_headroom_mb, model_load_time_ms.
- Alerts:
  - Latency SLO breach: p99 > configured_slo for 5m -> SEV2
  - Kernel tail regression: kernel_tail_ms increased > 25% vs baseline -> SEV3 (pager optional)
  - GPU OOM/driver reset -> SEV1 (page oncall)
  - KV cache checksum failures -> SEV1 (page oncall + applied-ml)

9) Team wiki & ownership
- Primary owners: serving-runtime team (rotation leads: Aisha Patel, Jonas Müller).
- Oncall: eng-sre (primary) with serving-runtime as secondary. See /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotations for schedule.
- Documents and related artifacts: model profiles in the model-catalog, benchmark results in s3://redwood-perf/serving-runtime/, and profiling artifacts in the traces bucket.

Useful links
- Serving runtime comprehensive: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-comprehensive-2026.json
- Runtime runbooks and playbooks: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-runbooks-and-playbook-2026.json
- Benchmarking suite repo: git@github.com:redwood/serving-benchmarks

Appendix: templates and example commands
- Capture profiler: rwi-profiler --model-profile gpt-3b-int8 --duration 300 --output /tmp/trace.json
- Run a microbenchmark: ./bench/run_benchmark --model-profile gpt-3b-int8 --seq-lens 64 --concurrency 32 --duration 300
- Emergency rollback env: export SCHED_POLICY=legacy; systemctl restart redwood-serving-worker
